title: Chapter Sixteen: The Town That Has to Be Rung

blocks.c: Chapter Sixteen: The Town That Has to Be Rung
They stayed nineteen hours, because the Sprat could not go up until the Gull came round again, and because — Sol suspected — Roake could not have got back in that boat if she had tried.
Sol spent the hours walking, and Lowspire let her.

She learned that the town rang twice a day: a full round at the sixth hour and a short round at the eighteenth, and that the whole population knew both by heart, and that the rounds were rung by four hands in rotation, all of them trained by Kerrin, the youngest of whom was nineteen and had been born on the platform.

She learned that the carry was rationed like water. Every hammer blow on the platform was logged. There was a smith, but the smith worked only in the four hours after a round, when the carry was at its fullest, because vibration bleeds it. There was a school but no bell in the school. There were two hundred and eleven people and not one dog with a loud bark; the dogs were selected for it, which was the single most unsettling fact Sol learned all day.

She learned that they had a tally. Of course they had a tally. It was kept in the chapel because that was the driest building, and it went back eleven years, and the marks were in four hands, and it was as thick as her fist.

She read a page of it standing up and found the eleven long rounds — the midsummer takings, the ones that had shown as dead on the Gull's book — and beside each, in Kerrin's writing, the same four words:
Taken. Recorded. Owed. Sorry.
Eleven times. The same four words. Sol stood in a cold chapel with her thumb on the page for a long time.
The school was in the chapel too, and school on Lowspire ran at night, and Sol got herself invited into it by the simple method of standing in the doorway until somebody took pity on her.

There were eleven children, aged four to fifteen, and one teacher, a woman called Ottilie who had been a governess in Antrell in another life and had come down the Low Stair in eighty-four for reasons Sol never learned. The lesson was arithmetic. The arithmetic was carry.

That was the thing that stopped her in the doorway. In Kettlemouth, a child of nine learns sums with apples and shillings. Here, a girl of about eight was standing at a slate working out how many hours of hold a short round buys in still air against a load of two hundred tons, and getting it right, and being corrected on her handwriting rather than her answer.

"They all learn it," said Ottilie afterwards. "They have to. There is no one else. If the four hands are ill at once, somebody has to be able to ring, and somebody has to be able to tell them whether it worked."
"Can they? Tell whether it worked?"

"Three of them can. Pel is nineteen and rings the sixth-hour round on his own. Marta is eleven and I think will be better than him." Ottilie looked at Sol with a sudden and unnerving directness. "You are the ear off the ferry."
"Yes."

"Then may I ask you something I have wanted to ask a qualified person for nine years?" She lowered her voice. "Is it bad for them? Growing up on a hold. Hearing it all the time, in the feet, day and night, from birth. Does it do anything?"
Sol opened her mouth to say no, and found that she did not know, and that nobody in the world knew, because nobody in the world had ever grown up on a platform held in the air by a bell.
"I don't know," she said. "I'd like to find out. I'd like to find out with them here rather than not here, if that's all right."
Ottilie laughed for the first time. "That," she said, "is the least reassuring reassurance I have ever been given, and the first honest one, so thank you."
Dov, meanwhile, had gone under the platform, because that is what Dov did, and came up grey to the eyebrows and unusually quiet.
"Tell me," said Sol.
"The frame's got four years in it. Maybe five."
"Four years of what?"

"Of metal. Not carry — metal." He sat down on a bollard. "Carry holds it up. Fine. But the whole structure is cinder-iron out of the local seam, and cinder-iron rots when it's held under load in wet air, and they are four hundred feet under a cloud, which is the wettest air in the world. Every stringer I put a pick into came away in flakes. They have been so careful about vibration for eleven years that nobody has noticed the frame is going soft."
"Can it be fixed?"

"Yes. It needs about two hundred tons of good iron, a forge that can run all day, and eleven months of hammering." Dov looked up at her. "Hammering, Sol. On a platform where a smith works four hours a day because a hammer bleeds the carry."
Sol sat down slowly on the bollard beside him.
"So they can't repair it," she said, "because repairing it would drop them."

"They can't repair it on the carry they steal. It's not enough. It has never been enough; it's exactly enough to stay still, which is the worst possible amount." He rubbed his face and made it worse. "Kerrin's been running the finest piece of engineering I have ever seen in my life for eleven years and she has built a machine whose only output is standing still, and in four years it comes apart, and I do not think she knows."

Sol thought about the chalk on the inside of a door, and the four words in the chapel tally, and a woman of seventy-one cleaning a sound-bow across the grain because she had nobody left to correct her.
"She knows," she said.
